passages.t: Judgment on the neighbors, and God guards his house
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden of the word of the LORD against the land of Hadrach and Damascus its resting place’ (verse 1). The word moves against Hamath, Tyre and Sidon (verse 2). Tyre has built a fortress and heaped up silver like dust, but the Lord will strip her and she will be consumed by fire (verses 3-4). Ashkelon, Gaza and Ekron will fear, a mixed people will live in Ashdod, and the pride of the Philistines will be cut off (verses 5-6).

God will remove the blood and unclean food from their mouths, ‘Then they too will become a remnant for our God’ (verse 7). And he will camp around his house, and no oppressor will overrun his people again (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
With chapter 9 the book changes. There are no dates, no visions and no interpreting angel; these are poetic oracles, headed burden. Whether Zechariah wrote them later in life, or later prophets did, is debated, and this site takes no side.

The judgment moves south down the coast and through Syria: Hadrach and Damascus, Hamath, then the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon, then the Philistine cities. Some scholars read this march against the conquests of Alexander the Great in 333 and 332 BC; others read it as God's judgment on Israel's old enemies, in the language of earlier prophets.

The surprise is verse 7. The Philistines are not only judged but cleansed, and become part of God's people, like a clan in Judah.
passages.later: Amos named the same cities in his words against the nations (Amos 1:3-10). Ezekiel spoke at length against Tyre's pride and wealth (Ezekiel 28:2-5).
passages.asks: Even the Philistines, Israel's old enemies, become a remnant for God. Ask who you have counted as beyond God's mercy. And ask what pride God may need to cut off in you.

passages.t: Your King comes, humble and riding on a donkey
passages.happening:
“Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem! See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (verse 9). God will cut off the chariot and the war horse, the bow of war will be broken, ‘Then He will proclaim peace to the nations’ (verse 10), and his rule will reach from sea to sea.

‘As for you, because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit’ (verse 11). The prisoners of hope are to return to their stronghold (verse 12). God will make Judah his bow and rouse Zion's sons against the sons of Greece (verse 13). The LORD will appear over them, his arrow like lightning, and he will shield them (verses 14-15). He will save them as his flock, and they will sparkle like jewels in a crown (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
A king riding a donkey was not a picture of weakness; the judges' sons rode donkeys, and Solomon rode David's mule to his anointing. But it was not a war horse. A king on a donkey came in peace, not conquest. This king comes humble, and he ends war rather than waging it: chariot and horse are cut off, and he speaks peace to the nations.

The blood of the covenant recalls the covenant made at Sinai, sealed with sacrifice. A waterless pit was a dry cistern, and the prisoners of hope are captives who still have a future.

Verse 13 names Greece. Those who hold that Zechariah wrote it place it in the early fifth century, when Persia was at war with the Greek cities; those who date the chapter later read it against Alexander's time.
passages.later: Matthew says Jesus' entry into Jerusalem fulfilled this verse: ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey’ (Matthew 21:5), and John quotes it too (John 12:15). Moses sealed the covenant with ‘the blood of the covenant’ (Exodus 24:8).
passages.hard:
Why does a chapter about a king of peace also celebrate violent victory over the nations?

The chapter holds both pictures side by side: the humble king who removes the war horse and speaks peace (verses 9-10), and the LORD who makes Judah his bow and his people like a warrior's sword (verses 13-15). Readers are right to feel the tension. Several points help. The warfare is God's own action against the powers that oppressed his people, not a license for human aggression; the victory comes as God appears over them, with lightning and trumpet, in the language of a storm. The judgment also has a purpose beyond destruction: even the Philistines become a remnant for God (verse 7).

Jewish and Christian interpreters have often read the two pictures together, with the peace of the humble king as the goal and God's defeat of oppressors as its means. The chapter gives no one a warrant to make war in God's name.
passages.asks: Zion's king comes humble, riding on a donkey, and speaks peace. Ask what kind of power you expect God to use. And ask what it would mean for you to be a prisoner of hope.
